newsitem.title: TURKEY: Greek minister says to work with Turks on ties.
newsitem.headline: Greek minister says to work with Turks on ties.

text.p: Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos said on Wednesday Greece would work with Turkey to improve relations, a day after he announced Athens would maintain its veto on European Union aid to Ankara.
Speaking in Istanbul after talks with Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, Pangalos said Turkey belonged in Europe.
"The future of Turkey is in the European family. We will work with dedication towards finding solutions and creating a climate of confidence," Pangalos told reporters.
"We shall do whatever possible to overcome the difficulties of the past," he said. "This is the wish of both our people."
He was meeting with Ciller on the sidelines of a meeting at the Black Sea Economic Cooperation (BSEC) forum.

On Tuesday, Pangalos said at a meeting of EU ministers in Luxembourg that Greece could not agree to unblock aid worth 375 million ecus ($424 million) over a dispute with fellow NATO member Turkey in the Aegean.
"We have repeatedly declared that we cannot accept Turkish behaviour vis-a-vis our sovereignty," he told a news conference in Luxembourg.
He said Turkey had to "withdraw the threat of war" over Greek plans to extend its maritime borders and must turn to international law to solve disputes in the region.
The veto dashed hopes of other EU members Athens would ease its stance against its rival.
Ciller, who earlier expressed disappointment at the veto, struck a conciliatory tone after the talks with Pangalos on Wednesday.
"I am very happy that we found the opportunity to listen to one another. I repeat that the Turkish people are pleased with visits like this," Ciller told reporters.
The EU aid to Turkey was promised to help Ankara meet the increased competition posed by the customs union with the EU which took effect in January 1996.
Despite the veto, EU officials reported some progress at the Luxembourg meeting.
Greece and Turkey formally agreed an approach to solving differences in the Aegean, where they almost came to blows last year over some uninhabited islets.
They agreed they would each appoint two non-governmental negotiators to submit a report in mid-June with recommendations for dealing with the situation.
Pangalos was scheduled to leave Turkey on Wednesday evening.
